title: Text: DET Bill Brown ↔ Anthony Fenech

content.text: Anthony - I have caught up reading the clips but didn’t see the word “propensity”.  I did however spot the “good” instead of “well” goof: April 2, when your story said “Although he was the loser, Ross pitched “good” enough to win.  Should have been “well” enough to win. I’ll keep my eyes open for other grammatical suggestions.
I think they edited it out
Even though I am unsure if I was using it properly

Understood.  Your sentence (above) is a good example of the use of these words.  They are all tendencies.  As I was taught, albeit long ago, a penchant is a positive tendency (a penchant for charitable work).  A propensity is a more neutral tendency (a for remaining silent rather than criticizing).  A proclivity is a more negative tendency (a proclivity for not telling the truth).  Since striking out is a negative tendency, I think it would be the best choice in the sentence above.

Btw, Gardy’s quotation above shows a classic boo-boo of the good/well situation: to be grammatically correct he should have said “Candelario has been swinging really well (not really good). Hope this helps.  All the best.
And I used it as a negative, not positive
From my raw copy - shield your eyes ...

Above it looks to me like you are using “proclivity” to describe Candelario’s tendency for drawing walks.  That’s a positive trait, though, and would better be described as his “penchant” for drawing walks.  Goodrum’s strikeout-happy ways would be a proclivity.
